Torana Build Exchange: The Night Before the Board

Ahmedabad, Sunday 15 November 2026. Torana's engineers can build almost anything in a fortnight. Its chief product officer has until nine tomorrow morning to explain why that has not helped.

1. Sunday night, Navrangpura

Ishaan Trivedi had been at the kitchen table since the children went up at half past nine, and by midnight he had rewritten the second slide of the board pre-read four times. The slide was titled "FY28 Product Investment" and it contained three options, a recommendation box he had left empty, and a number — ₹7.2 crore — that he was fairly sure was the wrong number to be arguing about.

The Torana Build Exchange board met at nine on Monday 16 November at the company's office off Ashram Road, with two of the five directors joining from Singapore and one from London. Nandita Saraf, Torana's co-founder and chief executive, had told him on Friday evening that the board needed "a clear ask and a clear story", and that the story the investors wanted to hear was that Torana's engineering organisation had become three times more productive in a year and would now convert that into market share before the pre-monsoon construction season.

The first part of that story was true. The second was the part Ishaan could not get himself to write down.

2. How Torana got here, and the decision that still binds it

Torana Build Exchange was founded in Ahmedabad in 2019 by Nandita Saraf, who had spent eleven years in cement distribution in Gujarat and Rajasthan, and Parag Doshi, an engineer from Pune. It was a business-to-business exchange for construction materials: cement, TMT steel bars, tiles, sanitaryware, paints, electricals and plumbing. On one side sat 2,140 authorised dealers and stockists carrying brands such as UltraTech, Ambuja, Shree Cement, Tata Tiscon, JSW Steel, Kajaria, Asian Paints and Havells. On the other sat 61,000 active buyers — small contractors building four-flat walk-ups in tier-two cities, mid-sized developers, and a growing number of interior contractors.

Torana did not hold inventory. It matched an order, arranged credit through two non-banking financial company partners, generated the GST e-invoice and e-way bill, and took a commission of between 1.6 and 3.4 per cent depending on category. In FY26 it had processed ₹4,180 crore of gross merchandise value and recognised ₹96 crore of net revenue. It competed, at different edges, with Infra.Market, OfBusiness, Udaan and Amazon Business, and with the enduring incumbent: a contractor's existing relationship with the dealer two streets away who gives him ninety days of credit and does not ask questions.

One decision from 2022 constrains everything Ishaan can do in 2026. To secure priority allocation from the large cement and steel brands during the shortages of that year, Torana signed three-year framework agreements with 140 anchor dealers across Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. The agreements contained a price-parity clause: Torana would display, for any given brand and grade in a given district, a single price to all buyers, with only volume slabs and a published distance-based freight adder permitted as variation. In exchange, the anchor dealers guaranteed fill rates during shortage.

To implement that, Torana's engineers built what everyone still calls the Price Book — a single canonical catalogue and pricing service through which every order passes. Dealer-specific and buyer-specific logic was deliberately excluded from the data model, because the contracts said it must be. The Price Book is now referenced by 41 internal services. The anchor-dealer agreements were renewed once and come up again on 31 March 2027.

3. The industry in late 2026

Indian construction had had a strong eighteen months. Cement volumes were growing in the high single digits, infrastructure spending was steady, and the residential market in tier-two cities — Surat, Rajkot, Nashik, Indore, Coimbatore — was where the volume growth sat. Regulation touched Torana at four points: GST and the e-invoicing regime, which its platform automated; the e-way bill system, which governed every truck it dispatched; the state RERA authorities, whose registration requirements shaped which developers could buy on credit; and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, which had forced a rebuild of its contractor onboarding flow in 2025.

Two market forces bore directly on the Price Book. The first was the Open Network for Digital Commerce, which Torana had joined as a seller network participant in 2026 and where catalogue and pricing had to be expressed in a protocol Torana's single-price model fitted only awkwardly. The second was the export desk, opened in April 2025 to sell Morbi tiles and sanitaryware to distributors in the Gulf and North America. Export pricing is negotiated per contract, per container and per currency. It could not be expressed in the Price Book at all, and had been run since inception on a spreadsheet by two people in Ahmedabad and one in New Jersey.

4. What happened, and what turned out to be wrong

In January 2026 Torana's engineering organisation — 96 people, split between Bengaluru (54), Pune (28) and Ahmedabad (14) — moved onto AI-assisted development. The transition was led by Vikrant Rao, VP Engineering, and it worked. Median time from an agreed specification to a production release fell from 6.5 weeks to 9 working days.

In March, Nandita announced an internal programme called Rann — a ninety-day sprint to "close every gap between us and anyone in this market". The belief in March, stated in the kick-off deck, was that Torana's constraint had always been engineering capacity, that the constraint had now been lifted, and that the correct response was to convert the lift into feature coverage before competitors did the same. Rann was extended twice and ran to September.

By 30 September Torana had shipped 214 customer-visible changes in nine months, against 48 in the whole of 2025. GMV grew 19 per cent year on year — in line with the 21 per cent it had grown the previous year, when it shipped a quarter as much.

Three things were believed during Rann and have since turned out to be wrong or at least doubtful.

First: it was believed that verification would keep pace because the tooling generated tests alongside code. On 11 September, a change to the freight-adder calculation — nine days of build, reviewed in forty minutes by an engineer who had not written it — mispriced 1,840 orders across four districts of Madhya Pradesh over six days. Torana issued ₹2.7 crore of credits. More seriously, because eleven of those orders had been priced below the district parity price, two anchor dealers in Indore wrote to Torana on 26 September citing the parity clause. Farida Kapadia's team had, as of 15 November, not resolved either letter.

Second: it was believed that adoption of the new features was strong, because the product analytics said so (Exhibit 2). In October, Dr Leena Varughese's team in Toronto found that the instrumentation for 130 of the 214 changes had been generated automatically alongside the feature code, and that a substantial share of the events counted as "used" fired on background prefetch rather than on a human action. She has not yet said how large that share is; her estimate has moved from "maybe a fifth" to "possibly more than half" in three weeks.

Third: it was believed that contractor satisfaction was stable. The manual survey in Exhibit 3 suggests it is not, though the survey has problems of its own.

5. The people

Ishaan Trivedi, Chief Product Officer, Ahmedabad. Joined 2023 from a Bengaluru logistics company. Position: uncommitted; suspects the ₹7.2 crore question is the wrong question. Incentive: his own credibility is attached to Rann, which he supported in March. Not saying: that he stopped reading the weekly Rann adoption report in July because he no longer believed it, and told nobody.

Nandita Saraf, co-founder and CEO, Ahmedabad. Position: take the capacity; the market is consolidating and coverage wins. Incentive: a Series D conversation is live at a valuation that assumes 30 per cent GMV growth in FY28; "engineering productivity tripled" is the strongest line in the deck. Not saying: that one of the two interested funds has asked, in writing, about Torana's incident history.

Vikrant Rao, VP Engineering, Bengaluru. Position: hire thirty engineers in Pune, where fully loaded cost is about 22 per cent below Bengaluru. Incentive: the tooling transition is his achievement and headcount is how it is scored. Not saying: six of his eleven principal engineers — the people who do the reviewing — have been approached by a competitor, and two have told him they are tired.

Farida Kapadia, Head of Dealer Network, Ahmedabad. Position: nothing may touch the Price Book before the anchor agreements are renewed on 31 March 2027. Incentive: she negotiated the 2022 parity clause personally and regards it as the reason Torana survived the shortage. Not saying: that four anchor dealers in Rajkot have already told her informally they will not renew on parity terms, because their own margins have moved.

Marcus Hoffmann, Design Director, Berlin. Position: radical simplification; the contractor app now has 34 entry points where it had 12. Incentive: design's influence has visibly fallen. Not saying: that of the 214 changes, 47 shipped without any design review at all, and that he agreed to that arrangement in April to keep Rann moving.

Dr Leena Varughese, Principal Data Scientist, Toronto. Position: stop and re-instrument; no decision taken on current telemetry is safe. Incentive: a large re-instrumentation project would be hers. Not saying: the freight-adder logic that failed in September incorporated a distance model her team shipped in July, and she does not yet know whether it contributed.

Ravi Subramanian, Head of Enterprise Sales, Edison, New Jersey. Position: build negotiated pricing for the export desk now; ₹34 crore of committed volume from Rafaya Contracting LLC in Dubai depends on it. Incentive: the export desk is his creation and 70 per cent of his variable pay. Not saying: the Rafaya contract carries a ₹2.1 crore penalty if Torana cannot invoice in dirhams against negotiated per-container pricing by 31 March 2027.

Shraddha Iyer, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Position: freeze releases for one quarter. Incentive: she carries the escalation load across eight time zones. Not saying: for her four largest overseas accounts she has been quietly running orders through a manual process outside the product since August, which is why their satisfaction scores look fine.

Jitendra Bhatt, CFO, Ahmedabad. Position: neutral on product, firm on cash. Incentive: fourteen months of runway at the current burn. Not saying: he has modelled a scenario in which Torana does not raise a Series D and must reach breakeven by Q3 FY28, and has not shared it with Ishaan.

Exhibit 1 is the slide Nandita wants at the front of the board pack, and read one way it is remarkable: cost per change down 80 per cent. Read another way it says engineering spend rose ₹7.5 crore, net revenue growth slowed from 24 to 17 per cent, and decision-to-live time fell by only 46 per cent while build time fell by 80. 7. Voices

Nandita Saraf, board pre-read comment, 13 November, 22:40 IST

"Ishaan, the story is: we tripled output, we learned what breaks, we are now fixing it and scaling. Do not lead with the incident. Lead with cost per change. The fund will ask about September — answer it when they ask, not before."

Vikrant Rao, engineering channel, 5 November, 11:14 IST

"Let us be honest about the eleven people who review everything that matters. We shipped 214 changes through eleven pairs of eyes. Adding thirty engineers in Pune does not add a twelfth pair. It adds more for the eleven to look at. I am still asking for the thirty because the alternative — telling this team we are slowing down — will cost me four of the eleven by February."

Marcus Hoffmann, email to Ishaan, 6 November, 09:02 CET

"Thirty-four entry points. A contractor in Nashik opens the app to buy cement and is offered credit, forecasting, a loyalty tier, a referral scheme and a tile visualiser. We did not decide any of this. We built it, one item at a time, and each one was defensible on its own. The sum is not defensible and nobody ever looked at the sum."

Ravi Subramanian to Ishaan, chat, 12 November, 21:50 EST

"Rafaya have asked twice this week. Three weeks of work, Ishaan. Three weeks. I have ₹34 crore committed and a penalty clause I would rather you heard from me than from Jitendra."

Farida Kapadia, note to Nandita and Ishaan, 9 November

"Whatever the lawyers say about a pricing layer, the anchor dealers will not hear a distinction between 'outside the catalogue' and 'a different price'. We are four months from renewal with 140 of them. Rajkot is already wobbling. I would not touch pricing in any form before April."

Dr Leena Varughese, note attached to the October telemetry review

"I want to be precise about what I do and do not know. I know the events are noisy. I do not know by how much, and I will not know before February without nine weeks of work. Until then, Exhibit 2 should not be used to decide anything. That includes deciding to stop."

Shraddha Iyer, Singapore, on the 4 November escalation call

"Can I say the unpopular thing? My top four accounts are not in the product. I take their orders on email and my team enters them. Their satisfaction is high because they are not using what we built. I have been doing this since August and I should have said so in August."

8. The options as Ishaan currently frames them

Option A — Convert the capacity. Ask the board for ₹7.2 crore, hire thirty engineers in Pune, clear the 61-item roadmap by the pre-monsoon season, and take the growth story to the Series D. The case for it is Exhibit 1's cost per change and Vikrant's retention argument. The case against is Exhibit 4: arrivals rising into a review pool of eleven that has already shrunk by one.

Option B — Stop and consolidate. Freeze new feature intake for one quarter, spend the ₹7.2 crore on review capacity, telemetry re-instrumentation and Marcus's simplification, and remove entry points rather than add them. The case for it is Exhibits 3 and 4 read together. The case against is that Exhibit 3 may be an artefact of who answered the phone in a bad fortnight, that Leena has explicitly said her data cannot support a decision to stop either, and that a freeze gives Ravi nothing before 31 March.

Option C — Make the one big decision. Commit three quarters to rebuilding the Price Book so that negotiated, segment-level and protocol-conformant pricing are all first-class, renegotiate the anchor agreements in March on new terms, and accept that little else ships until mid-FY28. The case for it is that every genuinely irreversible item on Exhibit 6 runs through the Price Book and that 2022's decision has now become the binding constraint. The case against is Farida's letter, Jitendra's runway, and the fact that the renegotiation Torana would be attempting from a position of a live parity dispute in Indore.

Ishaan wrote all three on the slide. Somewhere after midnight he also wrote, in the notes field where the board would not see it: "Is any of this the decision? 68% of effort on a 14% margin segment. Nobody asked me for that. It just happened."

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The board meets at 09:00 IST on Monday 16 November 2026 and expects a recommendation, not options. ₹7.2 crore is the envelope Jitendra has confirmed; anything larger requires the Series D, which is not signed. Runway is fourteen months at current burn. The 140 anchor-dealer agreements, with the parity clause, expire on 31 March 2027 and Farida's team needs a settled position by early January to begin renewals. The Rafaya Contracting LLC contract requires dirham invoicing against negotiated per-container pricing by 31 March 2027, with a ₹2.1 crore penalty. The two Indore parity letters are unanswered and legal has advised a reply within thirty days. ONDC catalogue v2 conformance has a network deadline of 30 June 2027. The review pool is eleven principal engineers, six of whom have been approached by a competitor. And the pre-monsoon construction season — Torana's heaviest trading quarter — begins in late February.

10. Questions for discussion

1. Reconstruct what Torana believed in March 2026 when it launched Rann. What was the implicit model of its own constraint, and what evidence did it have for that model at the time?

2. Exhibits 2 and 3 give incompatible pictures of the same nine months. What would you need to know to adjudicate between them, and what would you do if you could not get it before Monday? Is the last row of Exhibit 3 — orders up from 7 to 9 — consistent with either exhibit?

3. Exhibit 1 reports engineering cost per change falling from ₹116 lakh to ₹23 lakh. What does that metric include, what does it exclude, and who introduced it? What would a more honest version of the same slide show?

4. Torana's build cost fell roughly 80 per cent while its decision-to-live time fell 46 per cent. Identify every stage of Torana's pipeline that did not get faster, and say which of them is now setting the pace. Does the answer differ for the contractor app and for the export desk?

5. Six of the nine stakeholders are withholding something material. Take any three and work out how the decision changes if that information were on the table on Monday morning. Which withheld fact, if disclosed, would most change Ishaan's recommendation?

6. Ishaan's three options all allocate engineering capacity. His midnight note suggests the allocation he should be arguing about is across customer segments, not across engineering activities. What should he do on Monday morning, and what exactly should he say to a board that has been promised a growth story and a clear ask?

11. Quarter past one

At a quarter past one, Ishaan opened the file that Jitendra had sent at seven on Friday evening and had not mentioned since — a cash model with a tab labelled "no-D" that he had not looked at. He read it twice. Then he went back to the second slide, deleted the recommendation box, and typed a new title above the three options: "What we are actually choosing between".

He looked at it for a while. Then he deleted that too, because he did not yet know whether it was truer than what it replaced, and the board was in seven hours and forty-five minutes.

Sandhaan Compliance Cloud: Forty-Seven Features and Nothing to Show

Pune, October 2026. Sandhaan builds four times faster than it did a year ago and grows no faster at all. Its head of product has eleven days to say where ₹3.6 crore should go.

1. The Monday before the plan freezes

At ten past eight on the morning of Monday, 5 October 2026, Aparna Kulkarni was already at her desk on the seventh floor of Sandhaan Compliance Cloud's office in Baner, Pune, because the Singapore call started at half past. On 16 October, eleven days away and three weeks before Diwali, Sandhaan's leadership would freeze the plan for the January–March quarter and commit — or not commit — ₹3.6 crore to twelve additional engineers.

Aparna was Sandhaan's vice-president of product. The proposal for the twelve engineers was hers, drafted in August, and over the past fortnight she had stopped believing in it. The reason sat in a single slide she had built on Saturday: between April and September 2026 her team had shipped forty-seven customer-visible features, against eleven in the preceding six months, and every commercial number she cared about had stayed exactly where it was.

2. Sandhaan Compliance Cloud

Sandhaan sold statutory compliance software to mid-market Indian companies: GST return preparation and reconciliation against the Goods and Services Tax Network, e-invoicing through the Invoice Registration Portal, e-way bills, TDS filings, and the annual Ministry of Corporate Affairs submissions. Its customers were companies with ₹200 crore to ₹3,000 crore of turnover — auto-component makers around Pune and Chennai, speciality chemical firms in Gujarat, apparel exporters in Tiruppur — typically with a finance team of nine to thirty people and no appetite whatsoever for a filing being wrong.

Founded in 2018 by Aparna and a chartered accountant named Deven Phatak, Sandhaan had grown to 412 customers and ₹71 crore of annual recurring revenue by September 2026, with an average contract value of ₹17 lakh. It sat in a crowded and capable market. Larger finance teams often ran Zoho Books or TallyPrime for accounting and bolted compliance on top; ClearTax and a set of chartered-accountancy networks competed for the filing workflow; Razorpay and others touched the payments edge of the same finance stack. Sandhaan's claim was narrow and, so far, defensible: it reconciled purchase registers against GSTN data more accurately than anyone else, and it did so for companies with many GST registrations across states.

In February 2026, Sandhaan's engineering organisation — thirty-eight people split between Pune and a smaller pod in Bengaluru — moved wholesale onto AI-assisted development. The effect was not subtle. A module that had taken roughly nine weeks from agreed specification to production now took eight working days.

3. The situation

What Aparna knew, and what her Saturday slide showed, is set out in Exhibit 1. Shipping had quadrupled. Net revenue retention — the share of last year's revenue that this year's surviving customers still represented — had moved from 103 per cent to 101 per cent, which was within the range Sandhaan had seen every half-year since 2023. New logos per quarter were flat. Support tickets had almost tripled. And the median time to take a new customer live had gone from 21 days to 34, because implementation consultants now had a much larger product to configure and explain.

The views from around Sandhaan's map differed sharply. In Bengaluru, the engineering pod was elated and slightly bored: they had built everything on the backlog by July and had spent August building things nobody had asked for. In Singapore, where Sandhaan's customer-success lead covered eleven customers with operations across ASEAN, the complaint was the opposite — she could not keep up with release notes, and two customers had asked her to stop sending them. In Toronto, the data scientist who owned reconciliation matching had a different worry: the accuracy of the core match had not improved in a year, because nobody had been assigned to it while everyone was shipping surfaces around it. And in New Jersey, the sales head who covered Indian-headquartered groups with North American subsidiaries wanted one thing only, and it was not on the backlog.

That one thing was the multi-entity consolidation model. Sandhaan's data model assumed one legal entity per customer with multiple GST registrations under it. Groups with several legal entities — increasingly common among Sandhaan's larger prospects, and universal among those with overseas arms such as Mehran Trading FZE, the Dubai subsidiary of a Rajkot engineering group that had been in Sandhaan's pipeline for fourteen months — had to be run as separate accounts that could not be reconciled together. Rebuilding that model was estimated at two quarters. It was, unmistakably, a one-way door: every existing customer's data would have to be migrated, and the new model would constrain everything Sandhaan built for the next five years.

4. The people

Aparna Kulkarni, VP Product, Pune. Wants a plan she can defend to the board on evidence rather than on enthusiasm, and is uncomfortably aware that the twelve-engineer proposal carries her name.

Sameer Joshi, Director of Engineering, Bengaluru. Wants the twelve engineers. His argument is straightforward and not foolish: Sandhaan's competitors have the same tooling, so a build-capacity advantage is available to anyone who takes it, and a team that is not building is a team that is losing people.

Vidya Balasubramanian, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Wants a release freeze. She has eleven accounts, a two-and-a-half-hour time difference from Pune, and a spreadsheet showing that of the forty-seven features shipped since April, her customers had adopted nine.

Rahul Menon, Head of Sales (North America), New Jersey. Wants the multi-entity model and nothing else. He has ₹9.4 crore of pipeline that he says is blocked on it, including Mehran Trading FZE, and he has been saying so since 2025.

Deven Phatak, co-founder and CEO, Pune. Has told Aparna he will back whatever she brings, and has also told the board that Sandhaan's engineering productivity has quadrupled, which he now has to reconcile with flat revenue.

5. Exhibits

Exhibit 1 rewards slow reading. Build time fell by 84 per cent; elapsed time from idea to live fell by only 39 per cent, because building had never been the whole journey — specification, review, release and consultant enablement had not moved. Unreviewed changes now wait nine days instead of two, and the adoption row has collapsed: seven of eleven features found real users in the old regime, nine of forty-seven in the new one. 6. The options

Option A — Take the capacity. Hire twelve engineers, clear the 38-item list in two quarters, and match every competitor feature-for-feature. Upside: Sameer is right that the tooling is available to everyone and that a visibly building team retains talent; sales gets a longer feature-comparison sheet for Diwali-quarter renewals. Cost: ₹3.6 crore of salary, ₹2.9 crore a year of carrying cost, a review queue already at nine days receiving 32 per cent more arrivals, and implementation consultants already 13 days behind receiving more to configure.

Option B — Fix the constraint and prune. Spend ₹2.05 crore on verification, implementation and support capacity rather than on building. Freeze feature intake for six weeks, retire the features that fewer than 5 per cent of customers use, and set an explicit removal target. Upside: directly addresses the two rows in Exhibit 1 that deteriorated; onboarding time and support load should fall; keeps ₹1.55 crore unspent. Cost: no new capability at all for a quarter, a demoralising message to a proud engineering team, and nothing for Rahul.

Option C — Walk through the one-way door. Put the existing team on the multi-entity data model for two quarters, ship almost nothing visible, and migrate all 412 customers in the April–June 2027 window. Upside: unblocks ₹9.4 crore of pipeline, addresses the request with the largest customer demand, and simplifies rather than enlarges the surface. Cost: six months of invisibility during renewal season, a migration that touches every customer's filing data, and — if the model is designed wrongly — a mistake Sandhaan will live with until 2031.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Exhibit 1 shows build time falling 84 per cent and idea-to-live time falling 39 per cent. What accounts for the gap, and which specific stage of Sandhaan's process is now setting the pace?

2. Which of the forty-seven features shipped since April would you have expected to be worth shipping, given Exhibit 3's pattern of demand? What does the adoption row (9 of 47) tell you about how Sandhaan is currently choosing?

3. Sameer argues that because competitors have the same tooling, Sandhaan must take the capacity or fall behind. State the strongest version of his argument, then state what would have to be true for it to be wrong.

4. On 16 October, what should Aparna propose, and what evidence in the case supports it? What would you want to measure over the following quarter to know whether you were right?

8. A note for the learner

The lens that organises this case is a cost asymmetry. Putting a change in front of customers involves five costs: choosing what to build, building it, verifying it, committing to it in front of customers, and carrying it thereafter. AI tooling collapsed exactly one of those five at Sandhaan. The other four did not move, and two of them — verification and carrying — got worse because they scale with how much you ship.

A well-reasoned answer starts by locating the constraint rather than by picking an option. Exhibit 1 locates it twice over: unreviewed changes waiting nine days instead of two, and customer go-lives taking 34 days instead of 21. Those are queues, and adding twelve engineers adds arrivals to queues that are already backed up. The theory of constraints supplies the rule — improving a step that is not the constraint produces no system-level gain, only inventory in front of the real one — and Exhibit 1 supplies the inventory: 38 features that nobody adopted.

The second move is to sort decisions by reversibility. Exhibit 3 does this explicitly. Cheap building genuinely helps with reversible, low-consequence work: a vendor-wise ageing view can be built, tried and deleted with no lasting cost. It helps not at all with the multi-entity data model, which will cost the same to get wrong in 2026 as it would have in 2019. The asymmetry is not "everything got easier"; it is "the two-way doors got nearly free while the one-way doors did not move". That reframing is what turns Sandhaan's ₹3.6 crore question from a capacity question into a portfolio question.

One defensible path. Aparna proposes B and C together and declines A. Concretely: spend ₹2.05 crore on four verification and release engineers, three implementation consultants and two support staff, which takes review capacity from 18 to 31 items a week and should return the review queue to two or three days. Put twenty-two of the existing thirty-eight engineers on the multi-entity model for two quarters, with a written design review and a named approver before any schema is cut, because that is the one-way door. Leave the remaining sixteen on a deliberately small flow of reversible parity items — the six-day and four-day ones in Exhibit 3 with genuine demand — under a standing rule that anything below 5 per cent adoption after ninety days is removed. Hold the unspent ₹1.55 crore for two quarters.

The reasoning is that this converts Sandhaan's build-cost windfall into the two things it cannot buy any other way: a fixed constraint and an irreversible decision taken carefully. It gives Rahul his pipeline on a six-month horizon rather than never, gives Vidya a falling support load, and gives Sameer's team the most technically demanding work in the company's history, which is a better retention argument than volume. What it forfeits is the feature-comparison sheet for the Diwali renewals — a real cost, and the one Aparna should be honest with the board about. The measurement that would tell her within a quarter whether she was right is not features shipped; it is median review-queue age, median days to go live, and the share of features shipped four quarters ago still in use.

When Building Gets Cheap and Deciding Does Not

Two companies, one week apart in March 2026, discover the same thing from opposite ends: their build costs collapsed and their throughput barely moved. The argument of this page is that the collapse did not make anyone faster — it relocated the constraint, unevenly, and the unevenness is the whole subject.

1. Two rooms, two weeks in March 2026

On Wednesday, 4 March 2026, Devika Anand sat in a glass room on the fourth floor of Oormi Play's office in Lower Parel, Mumbai, with fourteen printouts spread across the table. Oormi Play was a regional-language streaming service — Marathi, Bhojpuri, Tamil, Kannada, with a growing Odia catalogue — carrying 41 million monthly active users and 3.8 million paying subscribers at ₹79 a month. It competed for the same evening hours as JioHotstar, ZEE5, SonyLIV, Sun NXT, aha and Hoichoi, and its entire commercial thesis rested on being better than any of them at putting the right four rows on a Bhojpuri-speaking user's home screen at 9 p.m.

The fourteen printouts were fourteen distinct home-screen designs that Devika's discovery squad had shipped to production between October 2025 and February 2026. Before the squad adopted AI-assisted development in August 2025, building a new recommendation surface — new ranking call, new row types, new instrumentation, new fallbacks for a 2G connection in Chhapra — had taken about five weeks. It now took three days. The squad had used that gift exactly as one would expect: it had built fourteen surfaces instead of three.

Aggregate day-7 retention across the fourteen: 32.1 per cent in October, 32.4 per cent in February. Within the noise. Devika's FY27 plan was due on 18 March and the draft on her screen requested twenty-two additional engineers.

Two days later and 700 kilometres south-east, Rohit Bhargava was having a quieter version of the same argument in Gachibowli, Hyderabad. Rohit was chief product officer of Nimitt Systems, which sold quoting, inventory and field-sales software to industrial distributors — the firms that warehouse bearings, fasteners, switchgear and lubricants and sell them to factories. Nimitt had 190 customers, ₹96 crore of annual recurring revenue, an average contract value of a little over ₹50 lakh, a seven-month sales cycle, and twenty-two customers who insisted on on-premises deployment because their own auditors required it.

Nimitt's build times had fallen almost as sharply as Oormi's: a new module that had taken fourteen weeks in early 2025 now took three. On 6 March, Nimitt's second-largest customer — a Ludhiana fastener distributor with ₹1,900 crore of turnover — had asked for a custom rebate-calculation module. Rohit's architect had estimated eleven working days. The commercial team wanted an answer by Friday. Rohit's difficulty was that the eleven days were now the least interesting number in the decision, and he could not yet articulate why.

Both companies had received the same gift. Neither had got faster in any way that mattered. This page is about why, and about what the two of them should do differently — which, it will turn out, is not the same thing.

2. The idea, its history, and the four schools that disagree about it

State the idea precisely, because almost every error downstream comes from a loose statement of it.

The total cost of putting a change in front of users decomposes into five components. Selection cost is the cost of choosing this change from the space of changes you could make — framing, scoping, arguing, saying no. Implementation cost is the cost of turning a settled choice into working software. Verification cost is the cost of establishing that what you built does what you intended and does not break what you already had. Commitment cost is the cost incurred at the moment of exposure — communicating to customers, training support, migrating data, accepting a contractual obligation. Carrying cost is the recurring cost of the thing continuing to exist: maintenance, support load, constraint on future changes, and eventual removal.

The empirical claim of this topic is that between roughly 2023 and 2026 generative tooling cut implementation cost for common software work by something on the order of 60 to 85 per cent, and cut the other four by very little — cutting verification cost, in many organisations, not at all or negatively. The consequence is not a productivity gain but a relocation: the component that governs throughput changes, and any practice tuned to economise on implementation becomes, overnight, an optimisation of a non-binding cost.

The intellectual lineage is unusually clean. Fred Brooks, in No Silver Bullet (1986), separated accidental complexity — the friction of tools, languages and environments — from essential complexity, the irreducible difficulty of specifying a conceptual construct, and predicted that attacks on the accidental would produce large gains and then hit a floor. Herbert Simon supplied the economics twice: in his 1955 and 1956 papers on bounded rationality and satisficing, which established that choosing is itself a costly activity with its own optimisation problem, and in 1971, with the observation that a wealth of information produces a poverty of attention and that the design problem is therefore allocating attention efficiently. Eliyahu Goldratt's theory of constraints (The Goal, 1984) gives the operating rule: improvement at a non-constraint produces no system-level gain, only inventory in front of the constraint. Gene Amdahl's 1967 argument caps the arithmetic. Donald Reinertsen's Principles of Product Development Flow (2009) supplies the queueing mathematics that makes the relocation non-linear rather than gentle. Carliss Baldwin and Kim Clark's Design Rules (1999) supplies the option-theoretic account of why cheap experimentation raises the value of modularity and of delaying commitment. And William Stanley Jevons, writing in 1865 about coal, supplies the awkward complication: when the efficiency with which a resource is used improves, consumption of that resource usually rises rather than falls.

Four schools of thought take this material in incompatible directions. They are worth stating as propositions each would sign, and propositions each would refuse, because practitioners in a disagreement are almost always standing in different ones without knowing it.

The four are not points on a spectrum. Relocation and Jevons disagree about whether judgement is automatable; Relocation and essentialism disagree about whether volume is good; scepticism disputes the premise all three share.

Devika, without having named it, had been operating as a Jevons industrialist since August — more surfaces, faster, in parallel. Rohit's instinct was carrying-cost essentialism, which is common among B2B product leaders who have inherited a ten-year-old codebase. Neither had measured anything end to end, which is the sceptic's complaint about both.

3. Mechanics, worked

Three pieces of formal machinery do most of the analytical work here. None is difficult; all three are routinely skipped.

The Amdahl decomposition

If a stage occupies fraction f of end-to-end elapsed time and is accelerated by factor k, the overall speed-up is 1 / ((1−f) + f/k). The point is that the answer is dominated by f, not by k, once k is large. At k = 5, an f of 0.6 gives a 2.1× speed-up; an f of 0.2 gives 1.19×.

Nimitt's nine weeks are customer security review, change-advisory-board scheduling and on-premises upgrade windows — almost none of it under Nimitt's control. Verification rose in both because volume rose and because reviewers no longer had the author's model of the code.

Read the last row. An 8.3-fold acceleration of implementation produced a 1.8-fold acceleration of Oormi's pipeline; a 4.7-fold acceleration produced 1.36 at Nimitt. If either had been told in advance that the return on their tooling investment would be 36 to 80 per cent of cycle time rather than 400 per cent, they would have planned differently. The gap between those two framings is where most of the disappointment in enterprise AI-tooling programmes lives.

The queueing non-linearity

The second mechanic is why the relocation is violent rather than gradual. Verification at both companies is a capacity-constrained service: a finite number of senior people can review a finite number of items per week. For a single-server queue with random arrivals, expected waiting time in queue equals the service time multiplied by ρ/(1−ρ), where ρ is utilisation — arrival rate divided by service capacity. That multiplier is nearly flat until about ρ = 0.7 and then goes vertical.

The managerial implication is sharper than it first appears. It is not enough to add review capacity proportionally to output; you must add it faster, because the cost of a queue is convex in utilisation. An organisation that lifts build throughput 3× and review capacity 3× will land at the same ρ and be fine. An organisation that lifts build throughput 3× and review capacity 1.5× has not halved its performance — it has, at these utilisations, multiplied its queue by eight or more.

The stock–flow identity

The third mechanic governs carrying cost. Let F be features shipped per year, d the annual rate at which features are removed or naturally retired, and S the stock of live features. Then the stock approaches a steady state of S* = F/d. Carrying cost is proportional to S, not to F.

Second-order effects follow from these three, and it is the second-order effects that separate a good analysis from a competent one.

Jevons. Cheaper building does not reduce the amount spent on building; it raises the quantity built and usually raises total spend, because latent demand for software inside any company is enormous. Devika's squad did not use its five-week saving to think; it used it to build eleven more surfaces. Expect this, and plan the governance before the tooling lands, not after.

Seniority inversion. The activity that becomes binding — reviewing work one did not write, and judging whether it should exist — is done disproportionately by senior people, and senior capacity cannot be hired at the speed junior capacity can. An organisation that responds to a build-cost collapse by hiring engineers is adding arrivals to a queue whose servers it cannot buy.

Evidence inflation. When a credible working demonstration takes three days, a demonstration stops being evidence of anything except that someone spent three days. Organisations whose decision culture ran on "whoever builds it wins the argument" lose their tie-breaker and usually do not notice for two quarters.

Rising option value. Baldwin and Clark's result — that modularity is valuable because it creates real options, and that the value of an option rises with the cheapness of exercising it — implies something counter-intuitive: when building is cheap, you should commit later, not earlier. Cheap exercise makes waiting cheap. The instinct to "just ship it, it only took a day" destroys option value precisely when option value is at its highest.

Decision latency becomes a competitive variable. If two competitors can both build a feature in a week, the one that can decide in a day beats the one that decides in a month, and decision latency is a property of organisational design — who may say yes, how many people must agree, how long the forum queue is — not of product management technique.

4. When the idea applies, stated as tests

The asymmetry is not a universal condition; it is a claim about a particular organisation's cost structure, and it can be checked. Four tests, each applied to both protagonists.

Test 1: was implementation a large share of elapsed time? If f was under about 0.25, the whole discussion is a footnote for you. Oormi passes clearly (f = 0.56). Nimitt passes marginally (f = 0.41), but nine of its thirty-four weeks sit outside its own walls in customer change-control, which caps any achievable improvement at 74 per cent of cycle time no matter what it does internally.

Test 2: is the marginal decision reversible at low cost? Oormi's home-screen variants are almost perfectly reversible — a configuration flag, a day's rollback, no customer told anything. Nimitt's custom rebate module is not: once a ₹1,900-crore distributor computes its channel rebates in Nimitt, the module is load-bearing, its data model constrains the next three schema migrations, and removing it is a contract renegotiation. The asymmetry pays out for Devika and barely at all for Rohit.

Test 3: can verification capacity scale with output? Oormi's verification is partly statistical and partly human; the statistical part scales — with 41 million monthly users, sample size is never the binding constraint — but the human readout and decision forum does not. Nimitt's cannot scale at all in the relevant horizon, because the reviewers are its four principal engineers and, for twenty-two customers, the reviewers are the customers' own security teams.

Test 4: is the marginal value of an additional shipped unit positive? Oormi's evidence says no: fourteen surfaces, no movement in day-7 retention. Nimitt's says yes but concentrated: three modules built in 2024 account for 61 per cent of the reasons customers give for choosing Nimitt over its rivals, and forty-one others account for none.

The idea is actively misleading in three situations. First, when the organisation's real constraint is demand rather than supply — a company that cannot sell what it already has does not benefit from building faster, and framing its problem as a build-cost story delays the sales diagnosis. Second, when quality is a step function rather than a gradient: in payments, clinical decision support or anything touching the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, an eighty-per-cent-correct artefact has negative value, so cheap production of eighty-per-cent-correct artefacts is not a gift. Third, when the cost drop occurred in a stage you do not own — a hardware company whose firmware team got faster while its injection-moulding tooling lead time stayed at fourteen weeks has received a gift it cannot spend.

5. Hard edge cases

Multi-product portfolios. Cheap building multiplies the number of products a company thinks it can support, and the cost that bites is not per product but per pair. Shared identity, shared billing, a common data model and consistent permissions across n products imply n(n−1)/2 consistency relationships: four products give six, nine products give thirty-six. A company that goes from four to nine products because each became cheap has increased its integration surface sixfold. Nimitt had quietly done exactly this, shipping three adjacent modules in 2025 that each now required its own pricing logic.

Two-sided markets. Here almost every consequential decision — take rate, ranking, who bears a cancellation, subsidy design — is irreversible in practice, because reversal requires re-earning trust on a time constant of months. The build cost of a ranking change is now trivial; the observation cost is one to two quarters and cannot be compressed, because the information does not exist until the time has passed. Two-sided businesses therefore get almost none of the benefit on their most important decisions and all of the clutter risk on their least important ones.

Regulated products. In India, a change to a lending product's underwriting logic involves the Reserve Bank's digital lending directions, an audit trail, and frequently a customer's own compliance sign-off; a change to a market-facing feature at a broker involves SEBI's system-audit regime. The build fell from six weeks to five days; the approval path did not move from eleven weeks. The correct conclusion is not that the tooling is useless — it frees engineers for the approval-path work — but that a plan built on internal cycle times will be wrong by a factor of three.

Hardware plus software. The bill of materials freezes, and the decision it embodies is then fixed for the product's life. Software teams attached to hardware teams experience the asymmetry most acutely: they can build anything in days, inside constraints someone chose eighteen months earlier and cannot revisit. The mature handling is to spend the freed software capacity on late-binding capability — over-the-air updates, configurability, telemetry — so that more of the product remains a two-way door.

AI-native products. This is the sharpest case, because here verification cost rises rather than merely failing to fall. A deterministic feature is checked by asserting outputs; a model-backed feature has a distribution of outputs and must be checked statistically, against a curated evaluation set. Building the evaluation set is selection work — deciding what "correct" means for a summarisation feature in Marathi is a product judgement, not an engineering task — and it does not get cheaper. For AI-native products the asymmetry is not 80/0; it is closer to 80 per cent off implementation and 40 per cent on to verification.

Organisational seams. The honest observation about mature companies is that what they say and what they do diverge here. They say they have empowered teams and removed gates. What they have actually built, almost universally, is a two-lane system: an informal fast lane for changes everybody agrees are reversible, and the old governance for everything else, with the lane assignment made by a senior person's intuition rather than by any written rule. This works surprisingly well and fails in one specific way — nobody has written down what makes something fast-lane eligible, so under deadline pressure genuinely irreversible changes get waved into the fast lane by whoever is senior and tired.

6. Nine nuances that separate expertise from competence

Flow and stock are different balance sheets

The competent practitioner asks what a feature costs to build; the expert asks what it costs to keep. Tell-tale sign in the wild: a planning document that contains build estimates and no retirement plan. The obvious reading — "it only took four days, so it is cheap" — is wrong because the four days are a one-time payment against an annuity that runs until someone deliberately stops it, and almost nobody deliberately stops anything.

Utilisation is convex, so "a bit busier" is not a bit worse

Experts watch review-queue utilisation the way a treasurer watches a covenant. Tell-tale sign: a team that says "we're at capacity but managing" while pull-request age has quietly gone from two days to nine. The obvious reading — that a 20 per cent increase in load produces a 20 per cent increase in delay — is wrong by an order of magnitude above ρ = 0.8.

Verification cost tracks consequence and non-determinism, never build effort

Most review policies were calibrated in an era when large changes took long to build, so effort was a workable proxy for risk. It no longer is. Tell-tale sign: classify last quarter's incidents by the build duration of the causing change; if the median is under a day, the policy is indexed to a dead variable.

Expect Jevons, not savings

Finance leaders reliably expect a build-cost reduction to show up as a smaller engineering budget. It almost never does. Tell-tale sign: a business case that promises headcount reduction from a developer-productivity programme. The expert's forecast is that volume rises to absorb the gain and that the visible cost shows up two quarters later in support, incident and infrastructure lines.

Demos have stopped being evidence

When a working prototype costs three days, the existence of a prototype tells you about an individual's enthusiasm, not about the idea's merit. Tell-tale sign: roadmap items that no one can attach a decision date or a decision-maker to, because they arrived via a demo. The obvious reading — "look, it already works, so the risk is gone" — confuses feasibility risk, which has genuinely collapsed, with value risk, which has not moved.

Cheap building argues for committing later, not sooner

This is the nuance most often got backwards, including by sophisticated people. If exercising an option is cheap, the option is worth more, and the correct response to a valuable option is to hold it. Tell-tale sign: a team that treats "we built it" as equivalent to "we chose it" and has no moment in its process where a built thing is either adopted or discarded. The expert builds more and commits less.

Comprehension has replaced authorship as the scarce cognitive act

Reviewing code one did not write is roughly two to four times more effortful per line than reviewing one's own, because the reviewer must reconstruct intent rather than recall it. Tell-tale sign: review comments that are almost entirely stylistic, which is what happens when a reviewer has run out of the attention needed to reason about behaviour. This is the mechanism behind the seniority inversion, and it is why "add more engineers" so often makes throughput worse.

The asymmetry is local, and if everyone has it, it is parity

A build-cost collapse available to your competitors is not an advantage; it is a change in the industry cost structure, and advantage accrues to whoever exploits it differentially — usually through better selection, not faster building. Tell-tale sign: a strategy document whose central claim is "we can now build X quickly", where X is something any competent competitor can also now build quickly.

Measurement must be idea-to-outcome, not diff-to-merge

Nearly all published productivity figures measure a window that begins after selection and ends before commitment — exactly the window that got cheap. Tell-tale sign: a "3× productivity" claim sourced from tool telemetry. The expert's counter-question is: what was your median elapsed time from a decision being taken to the outcome being observable, in the same two quarters? At Oormi that number went from 63 days to 51.

7. How the practice differs by product type and stage

In consumer products with large user bases the statistical part of verification scales freely, so the binding constraints become experiment interference and readout capacity. Oormi could run forty tests concurrently on 41 million users without sample-size trouble; what it could not do was allow forty simultaneous changes to the same home screen without the tests contaminating each other, and it could not hold more than six serious readouts in its Thursday decision forum. The constraint is attention, exactly as Simon said.

In B2B and enterprise, verification is human and the commitment stage is largely outside the vendor's control: security review, change advisory boards, customer upgrade windows. For Nimitt, nine of twenty-five remaining weeks were the customer's calendar. There is also a distribution constraint that has nothing to do with engineering — Nimitt's eleven customer-success managers could introduce perhaps two meaningful changes per account per quarter before attention was exhausted, which caps useful shipping regardless of build capacity.

Platforms face an extra term: every decision is an interface commitment, and interfaces are the most irreversible artefacts in software because other people's code depends on them. Cheap building lets a platform team produce interfaces faster, which is close to the worst possible use of the gift. Marketplaces, as noted, concentrate their consequential decisions in incentive design where observation time is irreducible.

In hardware and physical goods the asymmetry is genuinely smaller, and it is worth saying plainly rather than inventing a parallel: the dominant lead times are tooling, certification and supply, and a software team's speed does not touch them.

For AI products the picture inverts partially, as set out above: verification becomes the largest line rather than the smallest, and the evaluation set becomes the specification.

By stage: at seed and Series A, reversal costs are genuinely near zero because few customers depend on anything, and the dominant risk is building the wrong thing at all. Cheap building is close to a pure gift; the discipline required is only to avoid mistaking activity for learning. At growth stage — Oormi and Nimitt both — the installed base makes some things irreversible while the culture still assumes nothing is, and this is where the largest errors are made. At scale, selection was always the long pole because of the number of stakeholders who must agree, f is often 0.15 or lower, and the honest expectation from a build-cost collapse is a ten-to-fifteen per cent cycle improvement, which is worth having and is not a transformation.

8. Three worked examples

Example 1 — Oormi Play: the constraint was never statistics

Devika's team believed its experiment throughput was limited by traffic. The arithmetic says otherwise. To detect a one-percentage-point absolute lift on a 32.1 per cent day-7 retention baseline at 80 per cent power and 5 per cent significance, the required sample per arm is approximately 16 × p(1−p) / δ² = 16 × 0.321 × 0.679 / 0.0001 ≈ 34,900 users. Against 41 million monthly actives, Oormi could support well over a hundred such arms simultaneously if they did not interact.

The actual limits were elsewhere. Each test required fourteen days to observe day-7 and day-14 behaviour — irreducible. Tests touching the same home-screen real estate interfered, capping non-interfering concurrent home-screen tests at about nine. And the Thursday product forum, the only body empowered to act on a readout, could absorb six readouts in ninety minutes. Nine concurrent tests × 26 fortnights per year = 234 test-slots a year; six readouts × 48 weeks = 288 decision-slots. Build capacity in February 2026 was roughly 900 surfaces a year. Oormi had built a factory feeding a letterbox.

The proxy has broken, and the processes have not been rebuilt.

Example 3 — Anukram Systems: the approach applied badly, and the recovery

Anukram Systems, a Chennai company processing motor and health claims for general insurers, adopted AI-assisted development in January 2025 and drew the Jevons conclusion deliberately: more, faster, in parallel. In Q1 2025 it shipped 19 customer-visible changes; in Q2 2025, 61. It did not add review capacity, on the reasoning that the tooling also generated tests.

The recovery is more instructive than the failure. Anukram did not reduce build speed. It did four things: an eight-week intake freeze to drain the queue; removal of 38 low-adoption features to cut the stock; investment of the freed build capacity in an automated regression suite that raised review capacity from 18 to 34 items a week; and a written two-tier release policy specifying which changes could go out on automated checks alone. By Q2 2026 it was shipping 28 changes a quarter with a fifth of the incident rate. Note that it settled at 28, not 61 — the sustainable rate was set by what it could verify and own, not by what it could build.

9. Failure modes and their early diagnostics

Hiring into the wrong stage. Early sign: headcount and shipped volume both rise while elapsed idea-to-outcome time is flat. Diagnostic question: of the last twenty shipped items, what share of elapsed calendar time was spent waiting rather than working? Cost of catching late: a year of salary against a queue, plus the carrying cost the extra output generates.

Governing by build estimate. Early sign: prioritisation meetings that discuss effort and not carry or reversal. Diagnostic: ask for the five-year cost of the last approved item; if nobody has it, the process is pricing an obsolete variable. Cost late: a migration two years out that costs three times what it should.

Silent utilisation creep. Early sign: pull-request age rising while everyone reports being productive. Diagnostic: plot median PR age weekly; it is the cheapest leading indicator of the whole failure. Cost late: the Anukram sequence — incidents, service credits, attrition of the exact people you need to fix it.

Surface sprawl without a removal rate. Early sign: the product's settings page grows monotonically. Diagnostic: what fraction of features shipped four quarters ago is still present and used by more than 5 per cent of accounts? Cost late: a codebase where every change has thirty dependencies and estimates stop being meaningful.

Mistaking parity for advantage. Early sign: strategy language built around speed of building. Diagnostic: could a well-run competitor build this in the same time? If yes, what is the actual moat? Cost late: a year of roadmap spent on commoditised capability.

Fast-lane leakage. Early sign: an irreversible change that went out under reversible-change governance and nobody can say who approved that. Diagnostic: is the fast-lane eligibility rule written down and applied by checklist rather than intuition? Cost late: a data-model or pricing commitment made without deliberation, discovered when it must be undone.

10. Where experts genuinely disagree

Three disagreements here are real and unresolved, and a practitioner should be able to argue all sides.

Is verification automatable? The Jevons position, in its strongest form, holds that verification is exactly the kind of bounded, repeatable judgement that automated evaluation handles well, that Anukram's own recovery proves it by raising review capacity 89 per cent with tooling, and that the current bottleneck is a two-year artefact of immature evaluation practice rather than a permanent feature. Its evidence is the historical pattern of testing automation and the observable fact that eval-suite quality, not human review, already gates most AI-native releases. What would have to be true for it to be wrong: that a material share of verification is judgement about whether a thing should exist rather than whether it works — and that share, for now, is not shrinking.

Should volume rise or fall? The essentialist position, steelmanned, is that empirical feature-adoption distributions are brutally long-tailed — typically 20 to 30 per cent of features account for nearly all usage — that carrying cost is real and compounding, and that the sole rational response to cheap building is a smaller, better product with an aggressive removal rate. Its evidence is adoption telemetry and the observed relationship between surface area and change cost. Against it: the essentialist cannot explain how you learn which 25 per cent matters without building more than 25 per cent, and the cheapening of building is precisely what makes that search affordable. The unresolved question is whether search and stock can be decoupled — which is what a high removal rate is supposed to achieve, and which few organisations have demonstrated at scale.

How large is the effect, really? The sceptics' strongest case is that almost all quoted figures measure diff-to-merge and that credible end-to-end studies find lead-time improvements in the 10 to 35 per cent band, consistent with Exhibit 2's 1.36× and 1.80×. On this reading the entire discourse overstates a moderate operational improvement. The counter is that the distribution is bimodal: greenfield and prototype work genuinely shows five- to tenfold gains, mature regulated systems show almost none, and averaging them produces a number describing nobody. What would settle it is the one measurement almost no organisation has: median elapsed time from decision taken to outcome observed, tracked across the transition. Devika could produce it; Rohit, because nine of his weeks sit on his customers' calendars, could not.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this can recite that the constraint moved. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four observable ways.

They measure elapsed time by stage before proposing anything, and they are unembarrassed about spending two weeks doing it. They maintain an explicit decision portfolio — a written classification of the organisation's recurring decisions by reversibility and consequence — and they route governance by that classification rather than by size or seniority. They set and report a removal rate as a first-class operating metric alongside shipping rate, and they defend a capacity budget for removal work in planning. And they treat their own calendar as the scarce resource the theory says it is: a master of this material spends the majority of their week on selection and on verifying outcomes, and writes very little implementation detail, because the tooling now supplies it and their comparative advantage does not lie there.

The negative tell is equally reliable. Someone who has studied but not internalised it will agree enthusiastically that deciding is the hard part and then spend Thursday reviewing a specification's field-level detail.

12. What each protagonist decided

On 18 March, Devika submitted a plan requesting five engineers rather than twenty-two. Three went to experiment infrastructure — non-interfering assignment, automated readouts, a holdout — and two to platform work on the ranking service. She restructured the Thursday forum into two sessions and raised readout capacity from six a week to fourteen. She set a surface removal target: any home-screen variant not retained after two readouts would be deleted, not left behind a flag, with a target removal rate d of 0.6. Her argument to Oormi's chief executive was Example 1: the company had built a factory feeding a letterbox, and the cheapest available gain was to widen the letterbox.

On 13 March, Rohit declined the custom rebate module and offered the Ludhiana distributor a configurable rebate engine scheduled for October 2026, with a ₹40 lakh discount on the current contract as compensation for the wait. His reasoning was Exhibit 3: the eleven-day build estimate had made the request look free, and the five-year cost was ₹46 lakh against ₹38 lakh a year of at-risk revenue — defensible, but only if the module were general rather than bespoke, and generality was a design decision that eleven days did not buy. He also instituted, over some objection, a written rule that any change touching the pricing data model required a one-page decision record and a named approver, regardless of how long it took to build.

Discussion questions

1. Devika's five hires and Rohit's refusal both amount to declining to use newly available build capacity. Under what conditions is that the right call, and under what conditions is it simply conservatism dressed as analysis? What evidence would distinguish the two in each company?

2. Anukram recovered to 28 changes a quarter, less than half its Q2 2025 peak. Was 28 the right sustainable rate, or the rate its recovery measures happened to produce? What would you have measured in Q4 2025 to know the difference — and would Anukram's board have accepted the answer?

3. All three companies treat verification capacity as a constraint to be relieved. The Jevons school would say it is a constraint to be automated away within two years. If you believed that, which of Devika's and Rohit's decisions would you reverse, and what would it cost you if the belief turned out to be premature by three years?

13. Going deeper

How AI is reshaping the PM role — the parent statement of this shift; read it to see the same asymmetry expressed as a change in what the job consists of rather than as a cost structure. AI-assisted building — the supply side of the asymmetry; matters next because your estimate of k in the Amdahl calculation has to come from somewhere real. Reasoning about trade-offs — once building stops rationing choices, trade-off reasoning is the only rationing mechanism left. The prototype as the new specification — the direct consequence of evidence inflation: if a demo is cheap, what does a demo commit you to? Moats when features are cheap to copy — the answer to the parity problem raised in nuance eight. Roadmaps when build time collapses — a roadmap was partly a schedule of build capacity; this asks what it is now a plan of. Telling a capability shift from a fashion — the discipline that decides whether any of this is durable enough to reorganise around. Discovery when synthesis is cheap but evidence isn't — the same asymmetry on the research side, and the sharpest place to see the distinction between evidence-gathering and judgement. What a PRD becomes when the reader can build — the artefact-level consequence for selection work. Reviewing work you did not write — the skill behind the comprehension bottleneck and the seniority inversion. Velocity illusions and where the bottleneck moved — the measurement counterpart to this page, and the antidote to diff-to-merge claims. Taste and editorial judgement as the scarce skill — what selection consists of once feasibility stops filtering ideas. Analytics when anyone can query the data — the identical asymmetry applied to evidence: producing an answer got cheap, deciding which question deserved asking did not.

When Building Gets Cheap and Deciding Does Not

Bengaluru, February 2026. Vartika Commerce Cloud is shipping four and a half times as much software as a year ago, and losing customers slightly faster. Its head of product has eleven days to explain why.

1. The Thursday the backlog ran out

On the evening of Thursday, 12 February 2026, Meghna Rau was looking at a spreadsheet that ought to have made her happy. Meghna was head of product at Vartika Commerce Cloud, a Bengaluru company that sold order management, returns handling and warehouse allocation software to about 340 direct-to-consumer brands in India — the kind of brand that sells skincare or running shoes on its own website, on Amazon and Flipkart, and through a Shopify storefront, and needs one system to reconcile all three.

The spreadsheet said that in January 2026 Vartika's thirty-four engineers had shipped 23 customer-visible features. In January 2025 the same team, then thirty-one people, had shipped five. The change was not mysterious. Since September 2025 every engineer at Vartika had been working with an AI coding assistant, and the median time from an agreed specification to a demoable, tested feature had fallen from nineteen working days to four.

Two other numbers on the same sheet were not cause for celebration. Net revenue retention — the proportion of last year's revenue that this year's surviving customers still represented, after churn, downgrades and upgrades — had drifted from 108 per cent to 104 per cent. And the product backlog, which for three years had been a comfortingly full queue of 61 items representing roughly two years of work, now represented about eight months of work. For the first time in Vartika's existence, the company could plausibly build everything anyone had asked for, and then would have to decide what to do next with nothing to guide it.

Anand Kalyanpur, Vartika's chief executive, had drawn the obvious conclusion and proposed doubling engineering headcount: a ₹4.2 crore annual commitment, to be signed off before the board met on 23 February. Meghna had eleven days to say whether that was the right use of the money. What she suspected — and could not yet prove — was that the thing slowing Vartika down was no longer the building.

2. The idea: a cost asymmetry, not a productivity gain

The idea Meghna needed is best stated as an asymmetry between two costs that people habitually lump together.

Implementation cost is what it takes to turn a settled decision into working software: writing the code, wiring the integrations, producing the tests, handling the edge cases. Decision cost is everything else in the loop — the cost of choosing what to build from the space of things you could build, the cost of verifying that what came back is actually correct and safe, and the cost of living with the choice afterwards: supporting it, maintaining it, migrating it, and eventually removing it.

The claim of this topic is narrow and empirical. Between roughly 2023 and 2026, generative coding tools cut implementation cost for common software work by something like two-thirds to four-fifths. They cut decision cost by very little. Where two costs that used to be roughly comparable diverge sharply, the smaller one stops governing the system. Anything you were doing to economise on implementation is now optimising a cost that barely matters, and anything you were skimping on to save implementation time is now the thing that limits you.

None of the underlying reasoning is new, which is why it is worth trusting. Fred Brooks, in his 1986 essay No Silver Bullet, split software difficulty into accidental complexity — the friction of the tools and languages — and essential complexity — the irreducible difficulty of specifying what the thing should do. He predicted that attacks on accidental complexity would yield large gains and then stop, because the essential part would remain. Herbert Simon had made the more general point in 1971: when information becomes abundant, attention becomes the scarce resource, and the design problem becomes how to allocate attention. And Eliyahu Goldratt's theory of constraints, popularised in The Goal (1984), supplies the operational rule: improving any step that is not the constraint produces no improvement in the output of the system, only more inventory piled up in front of the real constraint.

The sentence Meghna could say in a board meeting without sounding glib: "Our cost of building fell by about eighty per cent. Our cost of being wrong did not move. So the money should go where being wrong is expensive, not where building is slow."

3. How it actually works

Read the diagram carefully, because the mechanics live in it. A feature at Vartika passes through four stages. Framing is the work of deciding that this feature, in this shape, for this segment, is the right thing: six days of customer calls, arguing with sales, and narrowing scope. Building is implementation. Verifying is establishing that the thing does what it claims, does not break the seventeen other things it touches, and does not create a support or compliance liability. Rollout is documentation, enabling, pricing, and telling the support team.

AI tooling compressed exactly one of those four. Building went from nineteen days to four, a reduction of 79 per cent. But the cycle only fell from 33 days to 21 — 36 per cent — because building had only ever been 58 per cent of the cycle. This is the arithmetic of Amdahl's law, stated for computer architecture by Gene Amdahl in 1967 and equally true here: the speed-up you get from accelerating part of a process is capped by the share of the process that part occupies.

The second mechanic is nastier and is the step practitioners most often leave implicit. Verification cost scales with output volume, not with build effort. Producing a change quickly does not make it faster to check. In fact Vartika's verification time went up, from five days to eight, for two reasons. There was more change arriving per unit time, so the regression surface grew. And the person verifying no longer had the mental model that came free from having typed the code — a reviewer who wrote something knows where the bodies are; a reviewer of generated code has to go and look.

The third mechanic is the one nobody puts on a chart: carrying cost. Every shipped feature is not an event but a subscription. It generates support tickets, occupies documentation, constrains the next schema change, and must be migrated or deprecated eventually. Carrying cost accumulates with the stock of shipped features, while build cost is paid on the flow. Cheapening the flow while ignoring the stock is how an organisation quietly converts an engineering team into a maintenance team.

The fourth, and the one a product manager owns: reversal cost. Jeff Bezos's 1997 shareholder letter, restated more sharply in 2015, divided decisions into type 2 — reversible, "two-way doors", where you can walk back through if you are wrong — and type 1 — irreversible, one-way doors. Cheap building reduces the cost of trying, which helps enormously with type-2 decisions. It does essentially nothing for type-1 decisions: a pricing change communicated to 340 customers, a database schema that eight integrations now depend on, a promise about data retention made to an enterprise buyer's security team. Those cost what they always cost.

4. The arithmetic, worked

Meghna did the calculation that changed Anand's mind, and it is worth following line by line.

Read the bottom line slowly. At the 2025 shipping rate, keeping the existing product alive consumed about three engineers — a rounding error in a team of thirty-four. At the 2026 rate, sustained for a year, it consumes fourteen. Vartika would have to hire roughly eleven engineers simply to stand still. That is most of the ₹4.2 crore Anand wanted to spend, and it would buy no new capability at all. The cheap-build gain, left ungoverned, converts itself into a maintenance bill.

Now change one input and watch the answer move. Suppose Vartika keeps building at 23 features a month but deliberately retires the ones that do not earn their place — running each new feature as an explicit trial and removing it within a quarter unless adoption clears a threshold.
