Notice which input mattered. Halving build time again, from four days to two, would shorten the cycle from 21 days to 19 — a 10 per cent gain. Moving the keep-rate from 100 per cent to 30 per cent freed nearly ten engineers. The high-leverage variable is not how fast you build; it is how well you decide what survives.

5. Nuances a learner has to absorb

Cheap to build is not cheap to own

The single most common slip is to price a feature at its construction cost. Construction is a one-time payment; ownership is an annuity. Once building is nearly free, ownership is essentially the whole cost, and a portfolio decision — what do we keep? — replaces a project decision — what do we build? Organisations that have never had to think about de-commissioning suddenly must, and most have no process for it.

The constraint moves; it does not disappear

Goldratt's rule is unforgiving: elevate a non-constraint and you get nothing but inventory in front of the real one. At Vartika the inventory was visible — thirty-one features sitting in a staging environment on 12 February waiting for someone senior enough to verify them and someone in sales confident enough to tell customers about them. The correct response to a moved constraint is to re-measure, not to re-apply last year's fix at larger scale.

Verification is a function of consequence, not of effort

How much checking a change deserves depends on what happens if it is wrong, and nothing about generative tooling changes what happens if it is wrong. A layout change on a marketing page and a change to how GST is computed on a return credit note need vastly different scrutiny, and they now take the same four days to build. Teams that verify in proportion to build effort — an old habit, and once a sensible proxy — systematically under-check exactly the changes that matter.

Some deciding did get cheaper, and confusing the two kinds is costly

This is the nuance that separates careful practitioners from slogan-repeaters. Decision work splits into evidence-gathering and judgement. Evidence-gathering — synthesising 200 support transcripts, building a throwaway prototype to see whether users understand a flow, generating three alternative designs to compare — has become dramatically cheaper, and that is a genuine gift. Judgement — deciding which customers Vartika wants to be indispensable to in three years, whether to take a position on a category, what to refuse — has not. The asymmetry is not "building cheap, thinking expensive". It is "building and probing cheap, committing and owning expensive".

Reversibility is the eligibility test

Cheap building helps exactly in proportion to how reversible the decision is. If the cost of trying falls and the cost of undoing stays low, you should try far more than you used to. If undoing is expensive — a public API, a pricing architecture, a data model, a partnership, a promise to a regulated customer — then cheap building has made you faster at walking through a one-way door, which is not obviously an improvement. Classify before you accelerate.

It tells you where cost is, not where value is

This framework is silent on the only question that ultimately matters: which of the things you could now build is worth anything. It relocates your attention; it does not aim it. A team that internalises the asymmetry perfectly and still has no view of its customers will simply be more efficiently directionless. Pair it with something that generates judgement — segment economics, a strategy, a point of view about the market — or it is an empty container.

What it is routinely confused with

Three confusions recur. The first is "AI replaces product managers", which reverses the conclusion: if the expensive half of the loop is choosing and verifying, the role that does those things becomes more load-bearing, not less. The second is "prototypes replace specifications", which is true for communicating a shape and false for committing to a contract. The third is treating this as a statement about AI at all; it is a statement about what happens whenever one cost in a coupled system collapses. Cloud infrastructure did this to provisioning in 2008; the same displacement followed.

Questions a thoughtful newcomer should ask first

Before acting on any of this, measure four things about your own organisation. What fraction of your cycle time was ever implementation? (If it was 20 per cent, the whole discussion is minor for you.) What is your keep-rate — what share of what you ship is still there and used a year later? Who verifies, and is that person a bottleneck? And what does a typical wrong decision cost you to reverse? Two teams with identical tooling and different answers to those four questions should behave completely differently.

6. How this differs by product type and company size

In consumer products, verification is largely statistical: you ship to 2 per cent of users and read the numbers. Cheap building therefore converts almost directly into more experiments, and the binding constraint becomes traffic — how many independent tests your user base can support in a quarter without contaminating each other. The decision problem becomes experiment prioritisation, and it is real: a consumer team with 40 ideas and capacity for 12 clean tests per quarter is deciding, not building.

In B2B, which is Vartika's world, verification is human and slow because the buyer is not the user and the cost of a visible defect is a renewal conversation. There is also a distribution constraint: Vartika's customer-success team of nine can meaningfully introduce perhaps three changes a quarter to a given account before the account stops paying attention. Shipping 23 features a month into a channel with that throughput produces shelfware, which is worse than nothing because it still carries.

In marketplaces, most consequential decisions are about incentives across two sides — take rate, ranking, subsidy, who bears a cancellation — and these are precisely the irreversible, high-consequence decisions in the bottom-right quadrant. Building a ranking change is now trivial; knowing what it does to seller trust over six months is not, and cannot be shortened, because the answer only exists after six months have passed.

Company size changes the mix sharply. In an early-stage company the dominant risk is building the wrong thing at all, and reversal costs are genuinely low because few customers depend on anything. Cheap building is close to a pure gift there: prototype widely, keep little, decide late. In a large company, the installed base makes almost everything partly irreversible, and the number of stakeholders who must agree — legal, security, support, finance, sales enablement — means framing was always the long pole. A 79 per cent cut in build time at a company where building was 15 per cent of the cycle produces a 12 per cent improvement, which is why large firms often report disappointing returns from the same tools that transform startups.

7. Common mistakes

Hiring into the wrong stage

Symptom: engineering headcount rises, shipped volume rises, cycle time is flat or worse, and a staging backlog appears. Misunderstanding: that output is limited by the number of builders. Cheapest diagnostic: take the last twenty shipped items and plot elapsed calendar time in each stage. If more than half the elapsed time is spent waiting — for a decision, a review, a sales enablement slot — the constraint is not capacity to build, and more builders will make the queue longer.

Measuring the team on throughput

Symptom: a dashboard of features shipped per sprint is the headline metric, and it is going up and to the right while retention is not. Misunderstanding: that flow is a proxy for value, which it was when flow was expensive and therefore rationed by judgement. Diagnostic: compute the keep-rate — of everything shipped four quarters ago, what fraction is still present and used by more than 5 per cent of accounts? Below about 40 per cent, throughput is measuring waste.

Letting verification follow build effort

Symptom: review comments cluster on large diffs and skip small ones; incidents originate disproportionately in "trivial" changes. Misunderstanding: that effort indicates risk. Diagnostic: classify last quarter's incidents by the build time of the change that caused them. If the median is under a day, your review policy is indexed to the wrong variable.

Treating a prototype as a commitment

Symptom: a demo shown to a customer on Tuesday appears on a roadmap on Friday without anyone having decided. Misunderstanding: that because a thing exists it has been chosen. Diagnostic: ask, of the last five things on the roadmap, who decided and on what date. If nobody can name a decision moment, the organisation is being steered by its own demos.

8. What good looks like

A team that has internalised this looks different in three visible ways. Its planning conversation is about a portfolio rather than a queue: what is coming in, what is being kept, what is being removed, with a stated keep-rate target. Its shipping policy is tiered by consequence rather than by size, so a reversible cosmetic change goes out in a day with automated checks while a schema or pricing change gets a written decision memo, named owner and a reversal plan. And its product managers spend most of their week on the two expensive activities — framing choices and verifying outcomes — rather than on writing implementation detail that the tooling now supplies.

Concretely, at a company like Vartika this looks like: a weekly forty-minute "keep or kill" review over the features that crossed ninety days; a one-page decision record for anything in the bottom-right quadrant; a customer-success throughput number treated as a hard constraint on releases, not an afterthought; and an explicit budget of engineering capacity reserved for removal work. None of that is exotic. It is simply what happens when an organisation starts economising on the cost that is actually binding.

9. What Meghna decided

On 21 February, Meghna took Anand a counter-proposal. Vartika would hire four engineers, not seventeen: two into verification infrastructure — automated regression and release tooling, to attack the eight-day check — and two into the customer-success side of rollout. It would hire one researcher and no product managers. It would set a keep-rate target of 35 per cent and instrument it. And it would spend the remainder of the ₹4.2 crore on nothing at all for two quarters, holding it against the possibility that the constraint moved again.

Her argument was the arithmetic in Exhibit 1 and the 36-per-cent line in the first chart. Doubling the team would accelerate a stage that was already 19 per cent of the cycle and would add eleven engineers' worth of carrying cost within a year. The four hires attacked the two stages that had grown. And the keep-rate target was the only lever in the model large enough to change the outcome.

What to learn next follows directly from the three things she left unresolved. If prototypes are now cheap enough to build instead of specify, what exactly does a prototype commit you to — the topic of the prototype as the new specification. If any feature can be copied in a week, what is left that a competitor cannot copy — moats when features are cheap to copy. And if build time no longer paces delivery, what is a roadmap a plan of — roadmaps when build time collapses. Underneath all three sits the discipline of telling a capability shift from a fashion, which is the question of whether any of this is durable.

Two questions to sit with.

1. In your own last completed project, what percentage of elapsed calendar time was implementation? If you do not know, what would it take to find out this week — and what would you change if the answer were 15 per cent?

2. Your organisation has a process for deciding what to build. Does it have one for deciding what to remove? If not, who is currently paying for everything you have ever shipped?
